'''Susan Franklin Wood''' (November 5, 1958 – January 17, 2025) was an American public health professional. She worked for the [[Food and Drug Administration]] from 2000 until 2005, when she resigned as a protest against the agency's delays in approving the [[morning-after pill]] for use without a prescription. She later served as director of the Jacobs Institute of Women's Health at the [[Milken Institute School of Public Health]].

== Background ==
Wood, a native of [[Jacksonville, Florida]], was born on November 5, 1958.<ref name = Gabriel>{{cite news|url = https://www.nytimes.com/2025/02/06/us/susan-f-wood-dead.html|title = Susan F. Wood, Who Resigned From the F.D.A. Over Plan B, Dies at 66|last = Gabriel|first = Trip|date = February 6, 2025|accessdate = February 6, 2025|newspaper = [[The New York Times]]|url-access = limited}}</ref> Her father was a surgeon.<ref name = Gabriel/> Wood graduated from [[Rhodes College|Southwestern at Memphis]] in 1980, where she studied [[psychobiology]], and earned her PhD in biology from [[Boston University]] in 1989, through the university's Marine Program at the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]].<ref name = Langer>{{cite web |last=Langer |first=Emily |date=January 23, 2025 |title=Susan Wood, FDA official who resigned over Plan B ruling, dies at 66 |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2025/01/23/susan-wood-fda-plan-b/ |website=[[The Washington Post]] |url-access = limited |access-date=January 25, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Biography: Susan Wood |url=https://1997-2001.state.gov/picw/acwbio_wood.html |publisher=The President's Interagency Council on Women |access-date=October 13, 2023}}</ref> She was a researcher at  [[Johns Hopkins School of Medicine|Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Wood, Susan {{!}} Global Women's Institute {{!}} The George Washington University |url=https://globalwomensinstitute.gwu.edu/susan-f-wood |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=Global Women's Institute |language=en}}</ref>

==Career==
From 1990 to 1995, Wood was science advisor to the [[Congressional Caucus for Women's Issues]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date= |title=Guest Speaker Bio - Dr. Susan Wood |url=https://www.nimhd.nih.gov/programs/edu-training/hd-seminars/2013/mar/bio-wood.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160709030826/http://www.nimhd.nih.gov/programs/edu-training/hd-seminars/2013/mar/bio-wood.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 9, 2016 |website=nimhd.nih.gov}}</ref> There, she helped draft the [[National Institutes of Health]] Revitalization Act of 1993, a law that required the inclusion of women and minorities in NIH research.<ref name=Langer /><ref>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date= June 10, 1993 |title= S.1 - National Institutes of Health Revitalization Act of 1993 |url= https://www.congress.gov/bill/103rd-congress/senate-bill/1 |website= congress.gov |publisher= Library of Congress |access-date= February 10, 2025}}</ref><ref name=Nichols>{{cite web |last=Nichols |first=Francine |date=January 2000 |title=History of the Women’s Health Movement in the 20th Century |url=https://www.jognn.org/article/S0884-2175(15)33790-4/fulltext |website=jognn.org |publisher=Journal of Obstetric, Gynecologic & Neonatal Nursing |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref>

She then joined the [[United States Department of Health and Human Services]], in the [[Office on Women's Health]], where she served as Deputy Director and worked on the team that created the National Centers of Excellence in Women’s Health.

From 2000 to 2005, Wood was Assistant Commissioner for Women's Health of the [[Food and Drug Administration]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Biography: Susan Wood |url=https://1997-2001.state.gov/picw/acwbio_wood.html |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=1997-2001.state.gov}}</ref> She resigned over delays in approving the over-the-counter us of the [[Emergency contraception|morning-after pill]].<ref>{{Cite news |date=November 25, 2021 |title=Is the Plan B battle over? Former FDA official Susan Wood hopes so. |language=en-US |newspaper=Washington Post |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/wonk/wp/2013/04/06/is-the-plan-b-battle-over-former-fda-official-susan-wood-hopes-so/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |issn=0190-8286}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Gress |first=Amy |date=June 17, 2005 |title=2005: Dr. Susan Wood |url=https://whistleblower.org/timeline/2005-dr-susan-wood/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=Government Accountability Project |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Susan Wood |url=https://rewirenewsgroup.com/authors/susan-wood/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=Rewire News Group |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Abortion Pill Opponents Seize New Chance to Target FDA Approval |url=https://news.bloomberglaw.com/health-law-and-business/abortion-pill-opponents-seize-new-chance-to-target-fda-approval |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=news.bloomberglaw.com |language=en}}</ref> While an advisory panel had unanimously endorsed a move to make the pill available without a prescription, the final approval was subject to considerable delay, a decision she attributed to political pressure from social conservative influences.<ref name = Gabriel/> In an email to her colleagues, she said that "scientific and clinical evidence, fully evaluated and recommended for approval by the professional staff here, has been overruled".<ref name = Gabriel/> Wood travelled extensively across the nation afterwards, explaining to the public in media interviews, lectures, and newspaper editorial board meetings the need for transparency and scientific integrity within government as well as advocating that emergency contraception be made available over the counter to women of all ages.<ref>{{cite web |last=Wood |first=Susan |date=February 28, 2006 |title=When Politics Defeats Science |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/opinions/2006/03/01/when-politics-defeats-science/601fd5c4-8f75-49c1-98ab-287748e6deb6/ |website=washingtonpost.com |publisher=The Washington Post |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last=Wood |first=Susan |date=December 9, 2011 |title=With the Plan B decision, the Obama administration broke its promise |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/with-the-plan-b-decision-the-obama-administration-broke-its-promise/2011/12/08/gIQAznYqiO_story.html |website=washingtonpost.com |publisher=The Washington Post |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref> The FDA finally approved full non-prescription use of the emergency contraception pill in 2013.<ref name = Gabriel/>

After leaving the FDA, Wood became a professor at [[George Washington University]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=O'Kelley |first=Connor |title=Public health school launches open online courses on opioids |url=https://gwhatchet.com/2016/10/10/public-health-school-launches-open-online-courses-on-opioids/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=The GW Hatchet}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Plan B gets new label by FDA to clarify it doesn't cause abortion |url=https://abcnews.go.com/Politics/plan-gets-new-label-fda-clarify-cause-abortion/story?id=95657885 |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=ABC News |language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Varney |first=Sarah |date=June 7, 2022 |title=Misinformation Clouds America's Most Popular Emergency Contraception |url=https://kffhealthnews.org/news/article/emergency-contraception-plan-b-private-equity-abortion-debate/ |access-date=October 13, 2023 |website=KFF Health News |language=en-US}}</ref> She contributed to research across a broad range of areas, including strategies for healthy weight maintenance in lesbian and bisexual women,<ref>{{cite web |last1=McElroy |first1=Jane |last2=Haynes |first2=Suzanne |last3=Eliason |first3=Michele |last4=Wood |first4=Susan |last5=Gilbert |first5=Tess |last6=Barker |first6=Linda |last7= Minnis |first7= Alexandra |date=July 7, 2016 |title=Healthy Weight in Lesbian and Bisexual Women Aged 40 and Older: An Effective Intervention in 10 Cities Using Tailored Approaches |url=https://www.whijournal.com/article/S1049-3867(16)30037-8/fulltext |website=Women's Health Issues |publisher=Jacobs Institute of Women's Health |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref> heart disease,<ref>{{cite web |last1=Hayes |first1=Sharonne |last2=Wood |first2=Susan |last3=Mieres |first3=Jennifer |last4=Campbell |first4=Susan |last5=Wenger |first5= Nanette |date=September-October 2015 |title=Taking a Giant Step Toward Women's Heart Health: Finding Policy Solutions to Unanswered Research Questions |url=https://www.whijournal.com/article/S1049-3867(15)00103-6/fulltext |website=Women's Health Issues |publisher=Jacobs Institute of Women's Health |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref> and adolescent behavior.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Landry |first1=Megan |last2=Vyas |first2=Amita |last3=Turner |first3=Monique |last4=Glick |first4=Sara |last5=Wood |first5=Susan |date=July-September 2015 |title=Evaluation of Social Media Utilization by Latino Adolescents: Implications for Mobile Health Interventions |url=https://mhealth.jmir.org/2015/3/e89/ |website=JMIR mHealth and uHealth |publisher=JMIR Publications |access-date=February 10, 2025}}</ref> She continued until 2022 to teach a course she developed in Women’s Health.<ref name=MilkenMourns />

== Personal life and death ==
Wood and her husband, Richard Payne, had a daughter.<ref name = Gabriel/> In 2017, they moved to Scotland, living in Tobermory on the [[Isle of Mull]]. After Wood’s diagnosis with brain cancer in January 2023, the family divided their time between residences in London and Tobermory.<ref name = Gabriel/> Professor Wood died from [[glioblastoma]] in London on January 17, 2025, at the age of 66.<ref name = Langer/><ref name = MilkenMourns>{{cite web |author=<!-- not stated --> |date=January 22, 2025 |title=Milken Institute School of Public Health Community Mourns the Passing of Dr. Susan F. Wood |url=https://publichealth.gwu.edu/milken-institute-school-public-health-community-mourns-passing-dr-susan-f-wood |website=Milken Institute School of Public Health |publisher=George Washington University |access-date=January 25, 2025}}</ref>
